Attend
uh-TEND
v.
From Latin attendere, to stretch toward, from ad and tendere, to stretch. Webster 1828: to go with or accompany; to be present at; to fix the mind upon; to listen. The Latin figure is a bow drawn toward a mark, and Scripture uses the word for the mind stretched toward instruction and toward the Lord.

Biblical Definition

Attend in the Authorized Version usually means to give the mind, not merely the body. Solomon’s repeated call to his son is the pattern: Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father, and attend to know understanding (Proverbs 4:1), and again, My son, attend to my words; incline thine ear unto my sayings (Proverbs 4:20). The verb is paired with inclining the ear, keeping in the midst of the heart, and not letting them depart from the eyes — a whole discipline of retention, and it is addressed to the young because the habit is formed early or not at all. Paul uses the word once, and decisively, in his teaching on singleness: this I speak for your own profit; not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction (1 Corinthians 7:35). The phrase names the great advantage of the unmarried state as Paul understood it — undistracted attention — and it is offered as a liberty and not as a rule, since he has just said he speaks by permission and not by commandment. Luke uses the word of Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul — the opened heart and the attending mind in one clause.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ATTEND as to go with or accompany; to be present at; to be present in business or service; to fix the mind or regard upon; to listen; to wait on. The mental sense is the biblical one.

expand to see more

ATTEND, v.t. — To go with or accompany, as a companion, minister or servant.

To be present at; as, to attend a meeting or a church.

To wait on; to serve; to accompany with solicitude.

ATTEND, v.i. — To listen; to regard with attention; as, attend to the words of the wise.

From Latin ad and tendere, to stretch — attention is the mind stretched toward its object, as a bow toward a mark.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 4:1 — "Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father, and attend to know understanding."

Proverbs 4:20 — "My son, attend to my words; incline thine ear unto my sayings."

1 Corinthians 7:35 — "And this I speak for your own profit; not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction."

Acts 16:14 — "And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul."

Psalm 17:1 — "Hear the right, O LORD, attend unto my cry, give ear unto my prayer, that goeth not out of feigned lips."

Modern Corruption

Attention has become the scarcest commodity of the age and the most deliberately harvested, and 1 Corinthians 7:35 names undistracted attendance upon the Lord as a thing worth arranging a whole life around.

expand to see more

Paul’s phrase is without distraction, and he treats freedom from distraction as a real good to be weighed when a Christian considers marriage. The observation is more pointed now than when he made it, because an entire industry exists to fragment attention and is paid by the fragment. Proverbs assumes a young man capable of attending to a father’s words, inclining his ear, keeping them in the midst of his heart — sustained, retentive, unhurried attention, which is the precondition of all instruction and of all meditation. A believer who cannot hold his mind still for twenty minutes will not meditate day and night in the law of the LORD, whatever he intends. This is not a counsel of technique; it is a matter of what a man’s soul is being trained by.

Acts 16:14 keeps the doctrine straight before the discipline becomes a work. Lydia heard us, and then whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul. The hearing was hers, the attending was hers, and the opening was God’s, and Luke puts them in that order deliberately. Nobody attends savingly to the gospel by an effort of concentration. The Reformed doctrine of effectual calling is exactly this verse: the outward word preached to everyone in the riverside prayer meeting, and the Lord opening one heart to receive it. Which is why a preacher prepares his sermon with all his powers and then prays as though nothing depends on them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qashab (H7181), to prick up the ears, to attend; Greek prosecho (G4337), to hold the mind toward, at Acts 16:14; euprosedros, well-seated beside, at 1 Corinthians 7:35.

expand to see more

Hebrew qashab (H7181) — to prick up the ears, to give attention; Proverbs 4:1, 4:20, Psalm 17:1.

Hebrew natah ozen — to incline the ear; the companion idiom in Proverbs 4:20.

Greek prosecho (G4337) — to hold the mind toward, to give heed; Acts 16:14, 1 Timothy 4:13.

Greek aperispastos (G563) — without distraction, undivided; a hapax legomenon at 1 Corinthians 7:35.

Latin attendere — to stretch toward; whence attention, tension, and intent.

Usage

"Attend to know understanding (Proverbs 4:1) — the mind stretched toward instruction."

"That ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction (1 Corinthians 7:35) — undistracted attention as a real good."

"Whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended (Acts 16:14) — effectual calling in a single clause."
